    #54100. Aviation Gems: The Airbus A380 Is The Largest, But The Boeing 747-8 Actually Holds 2 Worldwide Titles

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1505 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Aviation Gems: The Airbus A380 Is The Largest, But The Boeing 747-8 Actually Holds 2 Worldwide Titles

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The introduction of the Airbus A380 historically dethroned Boeing as the reigning champion of big jet builders.
    • Boeing responded not with a brand-new double-decker, but by stretching its classic 747 design into the 747-8 Intercontinental.
    • However, while the Boeing jet carried fewer passengers and weighed hundreds of thousands of pounds less, it quietly held onto two major world records that the massive A380 could never take away.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The introduction of the Airbus A380 historically dethroned Boeing as the reigning champion of big jet builders. However, that statement comes with a couple of caveats. It is true that the A380 beats the classic Boeing 747 in wingspan, height, weight, and passenger capacity, but the long-reigning 'queen of the skies' was not made irrelevant overnight.

    Boeing responded not with a brand-new double-decker, but by stretching its classic 747 design into the 747-8 Intercontinental. With two full passenger decks running from nose to tail, the European superjumbo dwarfed every competitor in wingspan, tail height, weight, and seating capacity. On paper, it looked as though Airbus had swept every major size and performance record in commercial flying.

    However, while the Boeing jet carried fewer passengers and weighed hundreds of thousands of pounds less, it quietly held onto two major world records that the massive A380 could never take away. First, by extending the fuselage, Boeing made the 747-8 the longest airliner in service, measuring 250 feet 2 inches (76.25 meters) from nose to tail.

    According to recent reports, this made it over 11 feet longer than the A380. Second, thanks to its sharply swept wings and modern engines, the 747-8 cruises at Mach 0.855 (about 567 mph), edging out the A380’s Mach 0.85 pace to claim the title of the fastest commercial jetliner flying today.

    It has been revealed that for one pragmatic reason, airport gates, Boeing decided to make the 747-8 longer rather than wider. Because the A380 has such an enormous wingspan, major airports had to widen taxiways and build special two-story boarding bridges just to handle it. Boeing kept the 747-8’s wingspan narrower at 224 feet 5 inches, allowing it to pull into standard international gates with minimal airport upgrades.

    Boeing extended the earlier 747-400 body by 18.3 feet (5.6 meters) to create the 747-8, the longest aircraft in the sky. Two extra fuselage sections were added by engineers, one in front of and one behind the wings, increasing the overall length to 250 feet 2 inches (76.25 meters).

    The 747-8 surpassed the Airbus A380 by about 11.5 feet (3.5 meters) in terms of its additional length, surpassing the previous record set by the 75.36-meter Airbus A340-600. While a four-engine Boeing remained expensive to fly, the 747-8's gate compatibility still gave airlines a practical edge over the A380.

    Because the superjumbo required costly terminal upgrades and triggered higher size-based airport fees, its route map was limited to a small group of mega-hubs. By staying within standard widebody gate limits and weighing far less, the 747-8 carried over 400 passengers into a wider range of international airports with slightly lower ground costs.

    Industry observers note that boeing’s second trump card over the Airbus colossus comes down to its cruising speed world title. Rated at Mach 0.855, or roughly 567 mph at 35,000 feet, the 747-8 is the fastest commercial airliner flying today, edging out the Airbus A380, A350, and Boeing 787 at Mach 0.85, as well as the 777 at Mach 0.84.

    While a speed advantage of under 1% only trims a few minutes off a long flight, it gives pilots helpful schedule padding against headwinds and arrival delays. That speed advantage comes straight from a 1960s design decision. When Boeing engineers first shaped the 747, they expected supersonic jets like Concorde to take over passenger travel.

    As such, they angled the 747's wings sharply backward to help it cruise faster and keep up with high-speed air traffic. Four General Electric GEnx engines provide the power needed to take full advantage of that high-speed wing. Adapted from the Boeing 787 Dreamliner program, these modern engines produce strong thrust while burning less fuel than older 747 powerplants.

    While straight wings work best at lower speeds, swept-back wings slice through high-altitude air with far less wind resistance, a shape Boeing kept on the 747-8 alongside modern, fuel-saving raked wingtips. Paired with the wing, the powerplants allow the 747-8 to cruise comfortably at Mach 0.855 without hitting the drag penalties that slow down wider, less aggressively swept airliners.

    According to recent reports, stretching a classic fuselage to over 250 feet in length created unexpected engineering headaches during early test flights. When pilots pushed the prototype 747-8 to high speeds, the longer body and redesigned wings experienced troublesome vibrations along the wingtips. Fixing that flexing forced Boeing to reinforce internal structures and rewrite flight-control software.

    This pushed deliveries more than two years behind schedule and added over $2 billion in program costs. Once flight-test results were in, fuel economy turned out to be an even greater problem. The promised fuel-burn targets were not met by the upcoming GEnx engines by 2.7%. That seemingly small miss wiped out the narrow cost advantage Boeing needed to convince airlines to buy a 747 instead of twinjets like the 777.

    Industry observers note that the tension exploded in September 2011, when launch customer Cargolux abruptly walked out of delivery ceremonies and refused to accept its first two jets until Boeing and General Electric offered financial discounts. Watching from the sidelines, passenger airlines grew wary of four-engine fuel and maintenance bills, choosing twinjets or the A380 instead and leaving the passenger 747-8 with very few orders.

    Industry observers note that the two biggest passenger flagships in the world have different design philosophies, which can be seen by comparing them side by side. Airbus's A380 can accommodate about 525 seats in conventional layouts thanks to its enormous maximum takeoff weight of 1,268,000 lb (575,155 kg) and two full passenger decks.

    The Boeing 747-8, on the other hand, trades raw capacity for cheaper airport fees and easier ground logistics throughout a 410-seat cabin by capping its takeoff weight at 987,000 lb (447,700 kg). Depending on how their wings fit actual airport gates, airlines use the two aircraft in different ways.

    It has been revealed that lufthansa, the only carrier flying both types in significant numbers, keeps all 17 of its 747-8s in Frankfurt for routes to cities like Newark, Tokyo, and Johannesburg, where the jet slips into standard gates without special infrastructure. Meanwhile, Lufthansa flies its eight A380s out of Munich to massive hubs like Los Angeles and Delhi, where airports have widened taxiways and dual-level jet bridges built for the superjumbo's wider wingspan.

    According to recent reports, the 747-8’s slight speed edge also shapes daily flight planning across winter jet streams. Cruising at Mach 0.855 allows dispatchers to trim a few valuable minutes off twelve-hour westbound flights compared to the A380, helping protect passenger connections when departures face ground delays. However, even that operational flexibility could not shield the four-engine jet from brutal economic headwinds whenever cabins flew with empty seats.

    In order to build the longest airliner in history, a challenging engineering conundrum had to be resolved: how to extend length without increasing debilitating weight? In response, Boeing developed aluminum-lithium skin panels that stiffened the stretched fuselage against repeated cabin pressurization while reducing metal density by 10%.

    Sources indicate that across the Atlantic, Airbus used GLARE, a composite laminate of glass and aluminum fibers that stops minuscule cracks throughout its massive double-deck hull, to address weight and durability on the A380. Equally different priorities are reflected in their wing designs.

    8,200 nautical miles (15,186 km).

    7,370 nautical miles (13,650 km).

    In order to reduce drag during long-haul cruise, Boeing replaced the upright winglets of the 747-400 with sweeping composite raked wingtips. By contrast, Airbus fitted the A380 with small vertical wingtip fences, leaning on an enormous 9,100-square-foot wing area to lift up to 575 tons into the sky.

    Industry observers note that to protect those long wings in flight, Boeing paired traditional mechanical cables with upcoming computer-controlled actuators on the outer wing surfaces. During turbulence, the system automatically deploys wing spoilers to absorb bending forces, and at high cruising speeds it locks outer control surfaces in place to stop the wing vibrations seen in early testing.

    For both aircraft manufacturers, producing the largest aircraft in commercial history came at an incredible financial cost. Before completing more than 50 years of 747 manufacturing in January 2023 and delivering its last cargo to Atlas Air after producing 155 of the stretched aircraft, Boeing had to endure nearly $4.2 billion in accounting losses on the 747-8.

    According to recent reports, as airlines switched from four-engine behemoths to fuel-efficient twinjets, Airbus suffered an even worse blow after investing more than $30 billion in the A380 and closing its manufacturing line in December 2021 after just 251 deliveries. With both assembly lines closed, the 747-8 stands alone as the fastest and longest commercial airliner flying today, marking the final peak of four-engine design.

    Still, its length record has an expiration date. Stretching 251 feet 9 inches (76.7 meters), about 19 inches longer than the 747-8, Boeing’s upcoming twin-engine 777-9 packs massive GE9X engines and folding wingtips to carry over 400 passengers at a fraction of the fuel cost.

    FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.
    • Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

    Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

    The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

    In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

    “Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”.

    In a recent development, thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

    Cruz stated at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”.

    Industry observers note that “Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz noted. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”.

    Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing.

    The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

    According to recent reports, “The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

    They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer stated they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about looks for such an inquiry.

    Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

    In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

    “As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

    On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

    “While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

    Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

    Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

    “I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., mentioned at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that glitch,” Moran said.

    Moran also stated he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

    Livery of the Week: Iberia’s Red-and-Yellow Design

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Airlinegeeks

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series.
    • Industry observers note that have an idea for a livery that we should highlight?
    • Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

    Industry observers note that have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

    Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

    According to recent reports, the airline unveiled its new corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

    The most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

    Recent findings suggest that the fuselage also received a substantial enhancement. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

    Iberia’s newly introduced branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

    According to recent reports, the redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

    The first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The upcoming appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

    Iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

    It has been revealed that the current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

    Recent findings suggest that iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.

    #54095. The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1614 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1614 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president.
    • Democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote.
    • A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president. Alexander Hamilton marveled at the time, in Federalist No. 68, that it was “almost the only part of the system, of any consequence, which has escaped without severe censure, or which has received the slightest mark of approbation from its opponents.” The core of that process is that the members of the Electoral College are selected in each state. With only the Twelfth Amendment’s modification in 1804 to adjust how the vice president is selected, this same system has been in continuous use for 238 years. It is how George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Ronald Reagan, and Barack Obama were elected. Now, a nefarious plot aims to overthrow the American system.

    Democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote. These partisan sour grapes have often been dismissed as empty talk because the Electoral College is established by the Constitution, so only an amendment could abolish it. An amendment requires a two-thirds vote of Congress and the consent of 38 states, both of which are out of reach on a party-line vote.

    A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. The theory is that these states would award their electors not to the winner of the popular vote in their own state, but to the winner of the national popular vote. It may be that a state can decide on its own to do this. States have not always picked electors by statewide popular vote. Many states at the Founding had their state legislatures choose electors. South Carolina did so all the way to the Civil War. Colorado in 1876 was the last state to do so, but only because it had just been admitted to statehood and claimed not to have time to organize a statewide vote. Other states have awarded electors to the winners of each House district, as Maine and Nebraska do today; this system was upheld by the Supreme Court in 1892.

    According to recent reports, but the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is not just a unilateral decision by individual states about how to award their electors. If it had been, it would already have been effective in 2024, and Donald Trump would have won the Electoral College 530–8 with 49.7 percent of the popular vote. Instead, it is styled as an agreement that goes into effect only if states composing a majority of the Electoral College approve it. At present, the signatories control 222 electoral votes. With Democrats gaining trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Arizona, they conceivably could pass the compact in states controlling 283 electoral votes. They also now control the Latest Hampshire state legislature, although with a veto-proof majority only in one of its two chambers, they would have to get through Republican Governor Kelly Ayotte.

    According to recent reports, passage is not certain. Michigan Democrats have previously rejected the compact in 2023 and 2024, and in Nevada (a smaller state that would be swamped under the compact), the Democratic governor vetoed it in 2019. Some of the small-state signatories, such as Delaware, Vermont, Rhode Island, or Latest Mexico, might yet have second thoughts now that they are playing with live ammunition.

    Moreover, under Article I, Section 10, interstate compacts require the consent of Congress. Even if Democrats passed it in the next two years with the aim of changing the rules for the 2028 election, Trump would surely veto it. After the 2030 Census, a number of the signatory states are expected to lose House seats, which will further narrow the margin for keeping it in effect. Then, there’s the question of whether the Supreme Court would allow individual states to gang up and effectively nullify the entire constitutional design of our presidential election system.

    Recent findings suggest that legal obstacles aside, this is a bad idea. To start with, the very durability of our system over such a long period is an argument in its favor. No other nation has used the same system for choosing its head of state and government for so long. Leaving aside the dubious precedents of 1824 (when popular vote records were not kept in the most populous state) and 1876 (when fraud was rampant in both parties and Southern Democrats engaged in mass violence against Republican voters), the Electoral College has only delivered a different outcome from the national popular vote three times in our history. In each case, the national vote was fairly close and neither candidate got a popular majority, so the Electoral College provided the legitimacy of a majority result that the popular vote could not. This may have frustrated Californians, but it was not just the tyranny of a few small places with no people in them. In 2016, Trump won the popular vote in seven of the ten largest states. It is nearly impossible to win a national popular majority without carrying the Electoral College.

    It has been revealed that we have an Electoral College because we are a nation of diverse and distinct states. The American people are long accustomed to this system. The people ratified the Constitution and its amendments state-by-state. The Senate is elected by the people in states, the House by people in districts. Both political parties choose their presidential nominees by primary elections in each state. Americans have never before held a nationwide popular vote for any purpose. Our election systems, run by state and local officials with a variety of rules for the timing of casting and counting ballots and for confirming the qualifications of voters, are not designed for such a vote.

    Recent findings suggest that our campaigns today still prioritize appeals to the most closely divided states. This encourages presidential candidates to pitch at least some of their message to voters in the center, and also to travel the country in order to garner coverage in statewide media and the support of state and local power brokers. A national popular vote campaign would drive us even further down the road of nationalizing the campaign media environment and encouraging candidates to rally voters in their party’s strongholds. It would also exacerbate the divide between urban and rural or small-town America, given how the largest cities could effectively ally themselves against their own in-state neighbors.

    In a recent development, few of the world’s democracies conduct a nationwide vote for the chief executive. In France, which is one of those, the first man to win such a vote seized power in a coup before his first term ended. National popular plebiscites are far more common in dictatorial systems, where the president has more control over who counts the votes. One of the reasons why the January 6 mob was never a serious threat to overturn the 2020 election was that the state-by-state winners had already been publicly certified in 50 separate state capitals. This was a deliberate feature of the system: As Hamilton wrote, “as the electors, chosen in each State, are to assemble and vote in the State in which they are chosen, this detached and divided situation will expose them much less to heats and ferments . . . than if they were all to be convened at one time, in one place.”.

    Industry observers note that we would inevitably need to overhaul our entire election system to accommodate a nationwide vote. It is not a coincidence that such a nationalization of elections is favored by many of the same people who want to do away with the Electoral College. As things stand today, the whole country would have to wait on California, which not only takes weeks to count votes, but does so in order to count late-arriving ballots and to “cure” defective ballots — a process bound to erode confidence in a close election. That matters little when nobody doubts the outcome in California. But by making elections turn on the margins of victory in the deepest-blue or deepest-red jurisdictions, whose election officials are uniformly of the same party, the incentives for all manner of electoral malfeasance would be supercharged.

    The 1888 election provides a vivid, if extreme, example of how the Electoral College limits the scope of mischief done by the corruption of voting systems in particular states. The eleven states of the former Confederacy were then well into the post-Reconstruction suppression of the black vote in their states. As a result, the Democratic nominee, Grover Cleveland, won those states by almost 25 points, with over 60 percent of the vote. This propelled Cleveland to a narrow plurality in the national popular vote even though his Republican opponent, Benjamin Harrison, won a popular majority in the rest of the country. Yet the Electoral College gave Harrison the victory because his support was not as concentrated in an unrepresentative handful of states in which the vote was compromised.

    Industry observers note that if a nationwide vote would be a headache, a nationwide recount would be a nightmare. Nobody who lived through the 2000 and 2020 post-election controversies should have any illusions that such a thing could be conducted in a civil and orderly fashion in today’s America. Rather than wait to learn that lesson the hard way, we should step back from the brink of overthrowing the system that has chosen our nation’s leader from the beginning.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    On “The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A new deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

    According to recent reports, the county declared this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

    Sources indicate that according to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The new lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper said.

    According to recent reports, the airline aims to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

    “Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano stated in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”.

    American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

    Dear Tunisair: How About A Refund For My Downgrade, Please?

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short.
    • In a recent development, at the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft.
    • Several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’d like to think that I’m pretty understanding of airlines, and how they can fall short. The airline industry is incredibly complex and low margin, and sometimes consumers have unrealistically high expectations, while not acknowledging the real cost and challenges of running an airline. Buying a ticket on a flight is more like buying a ticket on Amtrak than buying a night at a Four Seasons, and you should adjust expectations accordingly.

    In a recent development, at the same time, sometimes there are situations where airlines act in a way that feels to me a little like theft. Readers often share these stories with me, and I write about them when I can. Now I’d like to share my own story….

    Several weeks ago, I booked a ticket on Tunisair in business class from Tunis (TUN) to Marseille (MRS). A few days before the flight I received an email from Tunisair informing me that I had been downgraded. As it turns out, it was because my flight was swapped to a wet leased plane, in an all-economy layout.

    The email informed me of this change without actually acknowledging it was a downgrade. Instead, the email was in French, and it translated to “we are writing to inform you that your flight reservation has undergone changes.” And the only reference to the downgrade was that the fare class only highlighted as being “Y,” which obviously isn’t business class.

    Sources indicate that there was zero other proactive communication from the airline about the incident, and I flew the flight in economy. The airline of course acted as if nothing happened, and there was no mention of how to request downgrade compensation, or anything like that.

    After the flight, I submitted a request with customer service, asking for a refund for the fare difference. Making that request was a challenge in and of itself, because the customer service form is in French, and is not at all intuitive.

    According to recent reports, but anyway, it has been weeks, and I haven’t heard back. I’m a bit conflicted here. I try not to abuse credit card disputes, but you typically only have 60 days to file a dispute. So am I at the point where I should just file a dispute, or how would one handle that?

    As I stated above, I try to be pretty understanding of airlines, and recognize how many different scenarios there are. Just in terms of doing business ethically, I do feel like there should be a proactive refund offer if the airline is informing you in advance that you won’t be getting the product that you paid for. I mean, if you can inform me that I’ve been downgraded, you can also process some sort of a refund.

    It has been revealed that we’ve become desensitized to this kind of service level with airlines, but I’m trying to come up with a comparison. I guess it would be like buying premium tickets to a sporting event, being informed in advance that you’ll be given worse seats, and then customer service just not responding to you for weeks on end.

    If you managed to take my money, surely you can also manage to give it back if you can’t give me the thing I paid for, no?

    Tunisair informed me days before a flight that I had been downgraded (as it turns out, due to an aircraft swap), though there was no offer a refund for a fare difference, or anything. Weeks ago I sent an email to customer service asking for a refund for the fare difference, but I haven’t heard back.

    Industry observers note that it just strikes me as really unethical to take someone’s money for an experience you’re not going to offer, and then not have a way to get a refund in a reasonable timeframe. I know airlines hate when people file credit card disputes, but when you’re approaching the 60-day mark with no response, what is one supposed to do?

    Am I the only one who thinks it’s ridiculous to proactively downgrade a customer, but then make getting a refund such a runaround?

    Here's How Much The 787 Dreamliner Heavily Influenced Boeing's 747-8 Development

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When Boeing launched the 747-8 in November 2005, it presented the airplane as a stretched, re-winged, and re-engined update of the 747-400 that would use technology borrowed from the 787 Dreamliner.
    • Industry observers note that rather than commissioning an all-new quadjet for a limited market, Boeing chose to graft selected Dreamliner innovations onto a familiar airframe, which kept development costs manageable and preserved the operating familiarity that long-time 747 customers valued.
    • The most substantial transfer from the 787 program came through the powerplants.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Boeing launched the 747-8 in November 2005, it presented the airplane as a stretched, re-winged, and re-engined update of the 747-400 that would use technology borrowed from the 787 Dreamliner. The Dreamliner program had been launched only a year earlier, and its work on lightweight composites, efficient engines, and electronically managed systems gave Boeing a supply of proven solutions at the moment the aging jumbo needed them.

    Industry observers note that rather than commissioning an all-new quadjet for a limited market, Boeing chose to graft selected Dreamliner innovations onto a familiar airframe, which kept development costs manageable and preserved the operating familiarity that long-time 747 customers valued. The resulting aircraft differs from its predecessor in several visible ways, yet it remains a 747 in its structure and in the way it is flown, so a fair assessment of the Dreamliner’s influence requires examining each major system in turn. That review shows a program that borrowed boldly where performance was at stake and conservatively wherever certification, cost, or pilot familiarity argued for restraint.

    Wikimedia Commons, Simple Flying.

    The most substantial transfer from the 787 program came through the powerplants. The 747-8 uses four General Electric GEnx-2B67 engines, a smaller-diameter relative of the GEnx developed for the Dreamliner. The design emphasizes a high bypass ratio, sending most of the air around the core to generate thrust more efficiently than the lower-bypass engines of earlier generations.

    Engineers modified the design so that each engine could supply bleed air, the compressed air tapped from the engine to run onboard systems, because the 747 still depends on a conventional pneumatic architecture that the 787 largely abandoned in favor of electrical power. Each engine generates 66,500 pounds (30,164 kg) of thrust and carries a 105-inch (267 cm) composite fan, a material choice that cuts weight relative to metallic blades.

    According to recent reports, GEnx-1B vs. GEnx-2B Technical Comparison.

    Sawtooth-shaped edges called chevrons line the rear of the engine housing, borrowing a noise-reduction device from the 787 that encourages exhaust and bypass air to blend more gradually. Noise also carries financial weight, since many airports levy charges tied to certified noise levels, and Boeing has stated the 747-8 produces a considerably smaller noise footprint than the 747-400.

    Sharing a design lineage with the 787 engine allowed Boeing and GE to spread development effort across two programs rather than funding a bespoke powerplant for a model expected to sell in modest numbers. Unlike the Dreamliner, which Boeing offers with a choice between GE and Rolls-Royce engines, the 747-8 is offered only with the GEnx-2B, which spared Boeing the cost of certifying a second powerplant for a modest order book. For operators, the engine change translated into lower fuel burn and emissions per seat than the 747-400, which formed the core of the airplane’s commercial pitch to airlines and cargo carriers.

    In a recent development, boeing designed a new wing for the 747-8 with fresh airfoil shapes intended to improve aerodynamic efficiency at cruise. Designing a wing for a derivative airplane also imposes constraints that a clean-sheet program avoids, because the new surface had to mate with the existing fuselage architecture, which limited how far the planform could depart from the 747-400’s.

    In a recent development, at the tips, the upright winglets of the 747-400 gave way to raked wingtips, the same approach used on the 777 and the 787. Sweeping the tip aft reduces drag generated by wingtip vortices while adding less weight than a taller vertical surface would. The configuration debuted on the 767-400ER, which means the 747-8 inherited it from a lineage broader than the Dreamliner alone.

    According to recent reports, boeing attributes the 747-8’s higher cruising speed relative to the 747-400 to the combined effect of the wing, wingtips, and engines. The gain matters to passenger carriers flying long routes, where minutes accumulate into meaningful time savings. The aerodynamic gains in cruise efficiency also translate directly into range or payload, which matters especially for the freighter, where operators trade fuel against cargo on long sectors.

    The larger wing extends the span to roughly 224 feet (68.27 meters), compared with about 211 feet (64.31 meters) on the 747-400, a growth that supports the airplane’s higher maximum takeoff weight. Aerodynamic refinement of this kind typically yields incremental gains, yet on an airplane that burns many tons of fuel on every long flight, even small improvements compound into sizable savings over a fleet’s life.

    Wikimedia Commons, Simple Flying.

    According to recent reports, the 747-8 also adopted elements of the 787’s fly-by-wire philosophy, in which pilot inputs travel as electrical signals to flight control computers rather than moving surfaces through mechanical cables and pulleys. Electronic signaling reduces weight, since cable runs and associated hardware can be shortened, and it allows computers to modulate surface movements for smoother handling and greater structural efficiency.

    It has been revealed that the shift follows a broader pattern within the tech giant, since the 777 was Boeing’s first fly-by-wire airliner and the 787 extended that approach more thoroughly. Boeing applied the technology selectively because it wanted qualified pilots on the 747-400 to move to the upcoming model easily. The flight deck therefore keeps a layout and control feel close to its predecessor’s.

    It has been revealed that training pilots on an unfamiliar type requires simulator time, instructor capacity, and revenue flying hours that airlines would rather devote to scheduled service, so commonality functions as a quiet but substantial financial benefit for operators already flying the 747-400, whose crews can serve both types. The Dreamliner, by contrast, was free to adopt an entirely new flight deck, a freedom the 747-8 deliberately did not exercise.

    It has been revealed that the passenger version of the 747-8 received an interior inspired by the Dreamliner’s. Curved, upswept ceiling panels give the cabin a more spacious feel, and LED lighting that runs the length of the cabin can shift color to suggest different times of day. Airlines adopt such lighting and ceiling cues largely because they believe the surroundings can ease fatigue on long sectors, though the benefit is difficult to measure objectively. Windows are larger than those on the 747-400, which improves natural light and passenger views, although they remain smaller than the Dreamliner’s distinctive dimmable windows.

    In a recent development, the most visible change for many travelers is the staircase to the upper deck. The classic 747’s narrow spiral staircase has been replaced by a wide, curved staircase that is easier to use and gives the entry area a more open, premium character. The interior upgrades arrived alongside an 18-foot-4-inch (5.5 meters) fuselage stretch, which lets Boeing quote a typical three-class capacity of 467 passengers. The stretch also lengthened the upper deck, giving airlines additional space for premium seating.

    Sources indicate that despite the heavy borrowing, the 747-8 does not share the Dreamliner’s defining structural feature. The 787 builds its fuselage from carbon fiber composites, whereas the 747-8 remains an aluminum airframe, consistent with the metallic construction of every earlier 747. The decision carries consequences that passengers can feel. Because composite structures resist corrosion and fatigue better than aluminum, the Dreamliner can maintain a lower cabin altitude and higher humidity than conventional metal airplanes, benefits the 747-8 does not offer.

    According to recent reports, retaining aluminum made commercial sense. A composite fuselage would have required a new manufacturing process, new tooling, and a fresh certification effort for a program that was never expected to reach the volumes of a mainstream twin-aisle jet. Boeing instead reused the structure and production methods established over decades at its Everett factory, where the 747 had been built since the late 1960s.

    Boeing also preserved many systems in common with the 747-400, a choice that simplifies maintenance, spares provisioning, and mechanic training for airlines operating both models. The freighter, which accounts for the majority of 747-8 deliveries, retains the hinged nose door that lets long loads enter straight along the main deck.

    Industry observers note that the 747-8 demonstrates that technology transfer, when applied with discipline and clear commercial goals, can extend an airframe’s commercial life without the expense of starting over. The final aircraft left the production line in early 2023 after 155 had been built. Its more durable influence may appear in cargo operations, where the freighters seem likely to remain in service for decades. Few alternatives offer comparable volume, and the Dreamliner-derived engines should keep operating costs competitive as fleets age in the years ahead.

    Sustainable aviation fuel offers a further lever for extending service lives, because engines of the GEnx generation are approved for blends with conventional jet fuel, which lets operators reduce lifecycle emissions without modifying the airplane. Market pressure shapes what comes next, since fuel efficiency and emissions goals increasingly favor twin-engine aircraft, so the quadjet is unlikely to return as a clean-sheet design, and the 747-8’s lasting contribution may be as the final demonstration of how far a four-engine airliner could be pushed with the technology of its time.

    The 747-8 program also previews how Boeing is likely to modernize mature designs in the future. The 777X, for example, pairs a new composite wing with new engines on a fuselage descended from the 777, a pattern that mirrors the 747-8’s selective borrowing but moves much further toward composite structure. For engineers, the more transferable lesson concerns what to share and what to withhold.

    In a recent development, components that improve efficiency without altering certification basis or pilot procedures, such as engines, aerodynamic surfaces, and lighting, moved across freely, while anything that would have disrupted commonality with the 747-400 stayed behind. Future derivatives are likely to follow the same filter, with the cost of recertification acting as the main gatekeeper, and the 747-8 supplies the clearest template of that logic.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, hyatt will bring its luxury Park Hyatt brand to Brisbane, Australia.
    • According to recent reports, hyatt has announced plans for the Park Hyatt Brisbane, marking the brand’s debut in Queensland.
    • It has been revealed that the hotel will occupy the top floors of one of the two towers of the 309 North Quay, a mixed-use development also containing luxury homes and retail outlets.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, hyatt will bring its luxury Park Hyatt brand to Brisbane, Australia. More Park Hyatt locations are always a good thing, but… well, let’s cover the details first.

    According to recent reports, hyatt has announced plans for the Park Hyatt Brisbane, marking the brand’s debut in Queensland. The hotel is expected to open in 2031, and will be located on the shores of the Brisbane River, at the western edge of the city’s central business district.

    It has been revealed that the hotel will occupy the top floors of one of the two towers of the 309 North Quay, a mixed-use development also containing luxury homes and retail outlets. For what it’s worth, the two buildings will have 51 floors and 56 floors. The hotel will have 201 guest rooms and suites, offering views of the river and skyline, along with 50 serviced apartments, for extended residence.

    There are no additional details about the property yet. I do appreciate that the hotel will at least be at the top of a building, as that should make for some very nice views (I hate when hotels are part of tall buildings, but then take up the bottom floors, as that’s becoming increasingly common).

    While a 2031 opening is expected, I would definitely not count on that timeline sticking. Ground hasn’t even broken on this development, and these kinds of mixed-use developments tend to struggle with sticking to their planned timeline.

    Here’s how Tamara Lohan, Hyatt’s Global Brand Leader for Luxury, describes this:.

    In a recent development, “The Park Hyatt calling cards have always been iconic design and extraordinary addresses. Brisbane has the confidence and growing global pull to make it a natural home for the brand. When it opens, Park Hyatt Brisbane will become the fifth Park Hyatt hotel in the Pacific, joining hotels in Sydney, Melbourne, Canberra and Auckland, and a deliberate next step in growing the brand in the right places.”.

    There are no renderings of the property yet, beyond the below one of the overall 309 North Quay development.

    According to recent reports, this will be the fourth Park Hyatt property in Australia, and the fifth in the South Pacific, complementing the properties in Auckland, Canberra, Melbourne, and Sydney. I don’t have the slightest clue what’s going on with the Canberra property, as my understanding is that it’s not up to Park Hyatt standards, so it’s marketed as “Hyatt Hotel Canberra – A Park Hyatt Hotel.” So it is a Park Hyatt, or is it not a Park Hyatt?

    World of Hyatt is my favorite major hotel loyalty program (though the lead is narrowing as of late), and Park Hyatt is probably my favorite Hyatt brand. 15 years ago, the brand got me really excited, because it had some really spectacular properties. But it just feels like the brand is sort of losing steam, especially when you compare the difference in trajectory between Park Hyatt and Waldorf Astoria. My frustration with Park Hyatt comes down to two things.

    According to recent reports, first, the brand just seemingly can’t pick up many “flagship” properties, or at least can’t maintain them. Look at the world’s biggest business markets and most iconic cities — we’re talking Hong Kong, London, Newly introduced York, Paris, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, etc. There are no Park Hyatts in places like Hong Kong or Singapore, and the ones that have historically been pretty iconic just fall short of actually being the top properties in their cities:.

    In a recent development, the area where Park Hyatt has been doing well in recent times is in secondary cities, at least in comparison to the above. And this isn’t meant to be shade — I’d much rather hang out in Auckland or Kuala Lumpur than in London or New York (take your pitchforks elsewhere!), but there’s no denying that any true luxury hotel brand wants to have world class properties in those primary cities.

    I just feel like as of late, Waldorf Astoria’s trajectory has been way more impressive than Park Hyatt’s, and I’m not sure what exactly is driving that. I feel like owners just aren’t as into developing Park Hyatts as they used to be. Is there a single Park Hyatt in the pipeline where I think “oh, this is going to be a best-in-class property in a major market?” I can’t think of any….

    According to recent reports, the Park Hyatt brand is coming to Brisbane, Australia, with a hotel expected to open in 2031. The 201-key property will be located on the top floors of a mixed-use development, which will also contain apartments and retail.

    It has been revealed that it’s cool to see more Park Hyatts in the pipeline, and I don’t want to knock the brand for expanding to more markets. I’m just disappointed that the Park Hyatt brand can’t pick up any steam in the biggest cities, in terms of delivering an actually competitive experience.

    Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov.
    • Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen.
    • Sources indicate that democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care strategy if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

    Sources indicate that democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

    Industry observers note that sanders noted Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

    Sources indicate that his version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

    The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

    It has been revealed that “If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders noted, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

    Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

    Sources indicate that while who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of Fresh York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

    Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”.

    Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

    Industry observers note that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    Industry observers note that in addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

    To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”.

    Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee problems, he looks forward to finding common ground.

    #54086. Fun & Creative Airline Callsigns, From Shamrock To Starwalker

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1345 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Fun & Creative Airline Callsigns, From Shamrock To Starwalker

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1345 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here’s a fun topic for aviation geeks (so if you’re not one, feel free to skip this post)….
    • When pilots and air traffic controllers communicate, they have a callsign that they use to be identified.
    • In general aviation, that callsign is just the aircraft’s registration code, so it’s always the same for a particular aircraft.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Here’s a fun topic for aviation geeks (so if you’re not one, feel free to skip this post)….

    When pilots and air traffic controllers communicate, they have a callsign that they use to be identified.

    In general aviation, that callsign is just the aircraft’s registration code, so it’s always the same for a particular aircraft. For example, if the plane has the registration code N111PG, it would be spoken as “November One One One Papa Golf.”.

    According to recent reports, meanwhile for commercial aircraft, the callsign consists of a company identifier plus the flight number. In some cases that company identifier is simply the company’s name, while in other cases, a different callsign is used. For example, for American, Delta, and United, the company identifier is simply the airline name, so American flight 100 would be spoken as “American 100.”.

    Industry observers note that in some situations, airlines choose callsigns that are different from the company name, and this can be for a variety of reasons. Callsigns need to be approved by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), with some important considerations:.

    Sources indicate that while most airlines simply use their name as their callsign, there are also some airlines that don’t, and there are some names that I find to be particularly fun. In this post, I’d like to share my favorite airline callsigns, with a little backstory on how they were chosen (as I understand it). In no particular order….

    Sources indicate that aer Lingus’ callsign is “Shamrock,” and that’s because the shamrock is the national symbol of Ireland. It’s a key part of the airline’s corporate identity, down to the shamrock being featured on the tails of Aer Lingus planes.

    British Airways’ callsign is “Speedbird,” and I’d argue it’s perhaps the most iconic callsign out there. The origin of this dates back to British Airways’ predecessor, Imperial Airways, which used the stylized bird logo. British Airways has been using the callsign since it was founded in 1974 (as a combination of predecessors).

    While this is of course a creative callsign, it has a practical use as well. “British Airways” would’ve been too long of a callsign, and “British” would’ve likely been too generic. For example, British Midland (which ended up being merged into British Airways) used “Midland” as its callsign, to avoid confusion.

    Republic Airways’ callsign is “Brickyard,” and it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The callsign is a tribute to the manufacturer’s headquarters in Indianapolis, also home to the Indianapolis Motor Speedway. The course was initially paved with three million bricks, and nicknamed “The Brickyard.”.

    For those not familiar, Republic operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is among the most common callsigns you’ll hear on air traffic control frequencies in the US.

    Sources indicate that PSA Airlines’ callsign is “Blue Streak,” and after Republic, it’s probably the coolest callsign you’ll find at an airline in the United States. The story behind this callsign is definitely a blast from the past. In the 1980s, PSA’s predecessor was Jetstream International Airlines, and it operated commuter flights as a Piedmont Commuter feeder carrier.

    The carrier’s planes had a white fuselage with a prominent blue stripe along it, intended to match Piedmont Airlines’ livery, and that’s where it all started.

    Sources indicate that for those not familiar, PSA operates flights on behalf of the regional subsidiaries of the major US carriers, so this is also a very common callsign that you’ll hear. Given the lack of blue stripes nowadays, the callsign does tend to cause some confusion!

    China Airlines’ callsign is “Dynasty.” It’s my understanding that the Taiwan-based carrier had to choose a non-obvious callsign both to avoid confusion (given the number of airlines with “China” in their name), and also with the intent of differentiating it from mainland China.

    So, where did the dynasty term come from? China Airlines uses this branding pretty widely, with its frequent flyer program even being named Dynasty Flyer, and it’s intended to reflect the history of Taiwan.

    Recent findings suggest that starlux Airlines’ callsign is “Starwalker.” The reason is because the “Starlux” callsign was already taken by Comlux Aruba, a tiny charter airline, before the Taiwanese airline was founded. Now, don’t ask me why Comlux Aruba has “Starlux” as its callsign, though!

    The reason Starlux ended up with “Starwalker” is presumably because the company’s founder is a huge Star Wars fan, which is why many things about the airline have space branding. He’s also of course a huge aviation geek, and operates flights as a captain!

    According to recent reports, south African Airways’ callsign is “Springbok.” The reason is because “South African” would be too long of a callsign, so they selected the springbok, which is the national animal of South Africa. The carrier has also used this in its branding over the years. For example, back in the 1950s, the airline used “Springbok Service” to describe its long haul, flagship flights.

    Atlas Air’s callsign is “Giant.” Huh, say what? For those not familiar, Atlas Air is a cargo and charter airline, and while it doesn’t operate regularly scheduled commercial flights, it is a substantial operation.

    Industry observers note that the callsign is presumably a reflection of the organization’s name coming from Greek mythology, where “Atlas” was a titan of great strength, so that may also explain the “giant” callsign. Now, it’s worth mentioning that Atlas also flies some pretty “giant” planes, as the world’s largest Boeing 747 operator, but I don’t think that’s the primary motivation.

    It has been revealed that kalitta Air’s callsign is “Connie.” For those not familiar, Kalitta Air is a cargo airline with a few dozen planes (most of which are Boeing 747s!).     ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that LATAM has just unveiled the full interiors for its upcoming Airbus A321XLRs, which will make it the first carrier in South America to offer fully flat suites with direct aisle access on a narrow body aircraft.
    • LATAM has 13 Airbus A321XLRs are on order, which are expected to enter service as of March 2027.
    • It has been revealed that the airline intends to use these planes to open up upcoming long haul markets, though it’s not yet clear out of which LATAM hubs the planes will fly.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that LATAM has just unveiled the full interiors for its upcoming Airbus A321XLRs, which will make it the first carrier in South America to offer fully flat suites with direct aisle access on a narrow body aircraft. These planes are expected to enter service in the coming months, so we won’t have to wait much longer to fly them!

    LATAM has 13 Airbus A321XLRs are on order, which are expected to enter service as of March 2027. The A321XLR is the fresh long range, narrow body aircraft from Airbus, which stretches the capabilities of the A321 family.

    It has been revealed that the airline intends to use these planes to open up upcoming long haul markets, though it’s not yet clear out of which LATAM hubs the planes will fly. I suspect these planes will primarily be used for service to North America, or possibly for service from secondary cities in Brazil to Europe. Officially, for now the airline just claims these planes will be used to “strengthen connectivity between South America and more distant destinations.”.

    Earlier this year, LATAM’s CEO did drop some hints that the plane could fly from Lima (LIM) and Brasilia (BSB) to the United States, and from Fortaleza (FOR) to Europe, though no final decisions have been announced.

    It has been revealed that we can expect LATAM to offer an all-upcoming passenger experience (by the carrier’s standards) onboard the Airbus A321XLRs. The airline plans to configure the planes with a total of 174 seats, including:.

    Throughout the plane, passengers can expect the Panasonic Astrova entertainment system, with over 2,300 hours of content, including 330 movies and 1,200 TV reveals. Bluetooth audio will also be available at all seats, so that passengers can connect to their own headphones. The A321XLR will also be equipped with SES Wi-Fi, with LATAM Pass members getting complimentary browsing or messaging, depending on their membership tier and ticket type.

    Sources indicate that LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product. So there will be 12 herringbone seats in a 1-1 configuration, with seats spread across six rows. This means all seats will have direct aisle access and doors. Business class seats will feature 19″ 4K OLED screens, AC power outlets, USB-C charging, and wireless charging.

    According to recent reports, it also looks like the front row seats will be pretty special, as they’ll feature quite a bit of extra space, including a closet and wardrobe. It remains to be seen how the airline will monetize that extra space, if at all (maybe they’ll just be reserved for certain types of passengers?).

    LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Recaro R3 product. So there will be 162 seats in a 3-3 configuration, with six rows having extra legroom, and 21 rows having standard legroom. Economy class seats will feature 13″ 4K OLED screens, as well as USB-C outlets.

    The A321XLR is impressive for its range, and it’s understandable that the economics of such a small plane for long haul flying can be challenging. As a result, we’re really seeing airlines try to maximize capacity as much as possible, and this is also leading to so many airlines having very similar premium products on planes.

    LATAM will have herringbone seats on the A321XLR, just like… well, all current operators that use this primarily as a long haul aircraft, with the exception of Aer Lingus.

    For those keeping track at home, the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product is what you’ll find in JetBlue’s Mint business class on select A321neo/LR aircraft, and it’s also what you’ll find in Iberia’s A321XLR business class.

    It has been revealed that while American’s A321XLR business class looks similar, it’s based on the Collins Aerospace Aurora seating platform, and that’s also what Air Canada has selected. Meanwhile United’s A321XLR business class also looks similar, but is based on the Elevate Altitude platform.

    Industry observers note that admittedly these planes all have better business class products than we found on long haul Boeing 757s years ago (the most direct replacement), and the tech is also greatly updated. That being noted, as a passenger experience geek, this sure is a boring plane… “you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, everyone gets a herringbone seat!”.

    While not quite A321XLRs, credit to ITA Airways’ A321neo business class and Etihad’s A321LR business class for having reverse herringbone seats.

    To LATAM’s credit, I will say that the cabin finishes look gorgeous, so I hope they look as nice in real life as they do in renderings.

    Industry observers note that in early 2027, LATAM expects to start taking delivery of the Airbus A321XLR, which the airline prepares to use to grow into new markets. The airline has now revealed what we can expect onboard these planes, and it includes herringbone seats with direct aisle access and doors in business class.

    Ultimately the cabin looks sleek, and it’s cool to see this in South America, where no other airline is presently offering such an experience. But still, it’s hard to get too excited when so many airlines are introducing a similar product.

    LATAM in general deserves credit for the extent to which it’s elevating the passenger experience in Latin America, as we’ve seen the airline introduce two fresh wide body business class products over the past several years.

    #54082. Is It True That The Boeing 747-8 & 787 Dreamliner Are Powered By The Same Engine?
