    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Is It True That The Boeing 747-8 & 787 Dreamliner Are Powered By The Same Engine?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1350 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that it is true that both the 747-8, the final iteration of the Boeing double-decker, and the 787 Dreamliner, its latest and greatest clean sheet design, use the same engine.
    • It has been revealed that the 747-8 exclusively uses the GEnx-2B while the 787 Dreamliner is the only jetliner to ever be equipped with the GEnx-1B.
    • For airlines that operate both the 787 and 747-8, using the same engine family simplifies maintenance, parts inventory, and technician training.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that it is true that both the 747-8, the final iteration of the Boeing double-decker, and the 787 Dreamliner, its latest and greatest clean sheet design, use the same engine. However, each of these aircraft uses a different variation of that same turbofan that is tailored to its unique needs and engineering qualities.

    It has been revealed that the 747-8 exclusively uses the GEnx-2B while the 787 Dreamliner is the only jetliner to ever be equipped with the GEnx-1B. Boeing chose the GEnx for the 747-8 primarily to modernize the aging jumbo jet with next-generation technology. Both aircraft feature distinctive serrated chevrons on the engine nacelles, which mix hot exhaust with cool air to significantly reduce noise.

    For airlines that operate both the 787 and 747-8, using the same engine family simplifies maintenance, parts inventory, and technician training. The GEnx-1B is a larger, more powerful, and more-electric engine designed for a modern twin-engine jet. The GEnx-2B is a smaller, simplified variant that incorporates traditional pneumatics to breathe life into the older 747 systems while providing modern fuel efficiency.

    It has been revealed that while the GEnx-1B (787) and GEnx-2B (747-8) share a common high-pressure core and 80% of their Line Replaceable Units, they are distinct engines optimized for different aircraft architectures. The most fundamental difference is how the engines interact with the aircraft's internal systems. The GEnx family is designed to stay on wing 20% longer than previous generations, with some fleet leaders exceeding 30,000 hours without a major overhaul.

    Industry observers note that both engines offer approximately 15% better fuel efficiency than the older CF6 engines they replaced. Tom Levin, General Manager of the GEnx/CF6 engine product line at GE Aviation, commented on the engine's success when the 1,000th GEnx engine was developed in 2015.

    According to recent reports, “The GEnx was the fastest selling engine in GE’s history, and now it is the fastest production ramp up of a GE widebody engine program. The GEnx engine has proven itself with outstanding performance and reliability.".

    The 787 uses a bleedless architecture where most systems are powered electrically. The 747-8 uses a traditional bleed-air system to power environmental controls and start the engines, requiring the GEnx-2B to include bleed-air ports. The GEnx-2B has fewer stages in the booster and low-pressure turbine, optimizing it for a four-engine configuration.

    The Boeing 747-8, on the other hand, uses a traditional bleed air system. It must bleed high-pressure air from the compressor to power the 747’s pneumatic systems, including cabin pressurization and thermal anti-icing.

    Recent findings suggest that to fit the 747’s wing and ground clearance, the GEnx-2B has a smaller fan diameter, 105 inches, compared to the 787’s 111 inches. Because the 747-8 has four engines while the 787 has only two, the -2B is simplified internally to be lighter and more optimized for its lower per-engine thrust requirement. The -2B produces roughly 66,500 lbs of thrust, whereas the 787 variants can reach up to 76,100 lbs.

    Sources indicate that the GEnx-1B has more power because it is intended for a twin-engine aircraft (787) that must maintain performance in the event of an engine failure during takeoff. Because the GEnx-2B's power is distributed across four engines on the 747-8, its thrust rating is 66,500 lbf lower. Compared with older engines like the CF6, the GEnx-2B's technology improves fuel efficiency and cuts emissions by 15%.

    In contrast to the 1B, the GEnx-2B has de-staged components to maximize weight and performance for a four-engine setup. In contrast to the 1B's four stages, the 2B's low-pressure compressor has three stages. In the low-pressure turbine, the 1B has seven stages, whereas the 2B has six.

    Compared with the 747-8, the 787 Dreamliner delivers bettereconomics and is much more efficient in the widebody market, as it is a lightweight twin-engine composite aircraft. These engineering variations determine their efficiency and commercial success. The 747 uses about 3,800 gallons of fuel per hour, while the 787 uses about 2,900 gallons. The 787-9 is extremely efficient, using approximately 2.31 liters per 100 km per passenger, which is significantly better than the 747-8's 2.82 liters per 100 km per passenger.

    Industry observers note that boeing's Dreamliner also costs significantly less to operate, with a lower cost per available seat mile. Airlines typically prefer smaller twin-engine aircraft because they are less dangerous to fill and fly. The 787's design and performance have allowed it to thrive in the modern aviation market, while the 747-8 saw limited passenger orders before production ended in 2017 and the 747 assembly line fully shut down in 2023.

    In a recent development, the Dreamliner has essentially eliminated the conventional hub-and-spoke paradigm that made the 747 necessary. While the 747 required high passenger capacity to be successful, the 787's efficiency lets it cover the same distances with fewer seats, making it a better match for today's point-to-point market.

    The 787's efficiency allows airlines to launch newly introduced, nonstop point-to-point routes that would not have been economically viable with older, bigger, four-engine planes. Despite being more efficient than previous 747s, the 747-8 is still best suited to high-volume hub-to-hub services. Airlines such as United have made large 787 orders to replace a mix of 747s, 767s, and early 777s with a single, simpler aircraft family, resulting in significant cost savings for pilot training and component inventory.

    The 787 incorporates a large amount of carbon composite material, making it lighter, more resistant to fatigue and corrosion, and allowing for higher cabin humidity and lower cabin altitude, which enhances passenger comfort and reduces structural stress. The 747-8 is a development of a traditional aluminum design, with a heavier base structure.

    Industry observers note that lufthansa has incorporated the 787-9 to handle flights that need the same range but have about 70–90 fewer people, even though it is still a 747-8 operator. Because of this, even at off-peak times, the airline can maintain high load factors (percentage of seats filled). British Airways switched to the 787-10 for important transatlantic flights to Upcoming York and Chicago after retiring its entire 747 fleet. The 787-10 is 25% more fuel-efficient than the 747 while offering comparable cargo capacity and contemporary comforts.

    Compared to the 747, the 787 Dreamliner offers a better long-haul passenger experience because its composite airframe creates a cabin environment that more closely resembles ground conditions. When compared to older aircraft like the 747, which have a cabin altitude of 8,000 feet, the 787's cabin altitude of 6,000 feet makes a significant difference for passengers. That lower cabin altitude does many things to reduce the effects of fatigue on passengers inflight.

    Sources indicate that the composite construction of the 787 is not only 50% by weight but 80% by volume. Thanks to that light yet incredibly durable construction, it can do things no previous aircraft could. That includes having larger windows, higher humidity (15% or double that of legacy jets), and a more spacious interior with more natural lighting and better overhead storage.

    While the 747 is much loved for its incredibly smooth landing characteristics and gentle handling and flight, the 787 uses a latest technology known as 'smooth ride' to counteract turbulence in flight. This is the same technology that the 777X will use when it finally debuts in 2027. Although the 747 was known as the Queen of the Skies, the Dreamliner has become the best-selling widebody in history. It has been the flagship product of the legendary plane maker, as its 737 MAX has flailed in the wake of a disastrous debut.

    This is not only a major improvement for the long-haul market, but also for operators that use these aircraft for high-density hub-to-hub transport, and makes a major improvement for the densest routes in the world. A 787 Dreamliner is not only a game-changer for the operators that fly it, but it also marks a paradigm shift in the experience for flyers. While the era of the 747 ushered in a golden age of jet-powered commercial aviation, the 787 and future successors such as the 777X herald the next era in air travel.

    • The Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card launched in March 2026.

    • Recent findings suggest that this post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card launched in March 2026. On the surface, the card sounds rather uncompetitive — it has a $295 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers “just” 2% cash back on everyday spending, with limited bonus categories.

    Industry observers note that however, there are some things that could make this card worthwhile, including a potentially lucrative welcome offer, a solid return on spending, and some credits that can help offset the annual fee. If your business spends a lot, you value having an Amex, and you just want to earn simple cash back without a complex rewards structure, this could be a good option.

    Recent findings suggest that this post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review. Is the card worth it, and if so, under what circumstances? And what are the best alternatives?

    Link: Learn more about the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card.

    Before I get into my Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review, let me briefly summarize the key details of the card:.

    Beyond that, here are what I consider to be some of the major pros and cons of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited:.

    Industry observers note that with the above out of the way, let’s look at the various aspects of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, from the welcome offer, to the fees, to the rewards structure, to the other perks. This card is fairly straightforward, so there’s not all that much to understand, for better or worse.

    In a recent development, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited currently has a welcome offer where you can earn as high as $2,000 cash back after spending $50,000 within the first six months on eligible purchases. Reward Dollars can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases.

    Given that the card ordinarily offers at least 2% cash back, that means spending $50,000 could earn you a minimum of $3,000 (if offered the full bonus amount), equivalent to 6% cash back on that amount of spending, which is solid.

    Admittedly the spending requirement is big (it averages out to $8,333 per month over the course of six months), but I do think businesses that spend a lot might find this to be achievable. Furthermore, it’s nice that you have six months to complete the spending requirement, while many other cards give you only three months to reach the spending requirement.

    If you’re applying for the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, be aware of Amex’s general restrictions on applying for cards, including the “once in a lifetime rule.” That means you’re not eligible for the welcome offer on the card if you’ve already had this card, though you are potentially eligible for the bonus if you’ve had other Amex cards.

    Sources indicate that anecdotally, I find Amex business cards to be quite easy to get approved for. I also love how with Amex, you can know if you’ll be approved with no credit score impact — the hard pull only happens after you’re told if you’re approved, and you accept the offer.

    Also keep in mind that if you’re concerned about staying under Chase’s 5/24 limit, applying for an Amex business card won’t count toward that, since it doesn’t show up on your personal credit report in that way.

    In a recent development, when it comes to credit score, there’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the card, as it’s one of only many factors that determines eligibility. Personally, I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an annual fee of $295 (Rates & Fees), which is definitely on the steep side, especially given the relatively narrow appeal of the credits offered on the card, which require a lot of spending.

    With the card’s 2% cash back rewards structure, you’d essentially recoup the annual fee (in terms of rewards) after $14,750 in spending.

    According to recent reports, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an authorized user fee of $95 for the first 5 cards, and a $95 annual fee for each thereafter (Rates & Fees), though you can also get a no annual fee Employee Business Expense Card with no additional fee.     Restored to Calder’s initiative, the clouds are spinning again

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday.
    • The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.
    • In a recent development, fifty years later, Alexander S.C.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

    In a recent development, fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

    Recent findings suggest that “It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”.

    Industry observers note that it was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

    Sources indicate that rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

    According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”.

    Industry observers note that “It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he noted. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”.

    It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

    Industry observers note that “We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he said. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”.

    Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and remarked he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

    “We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how substantial this was until it revealed up on their doorstep.”.

    Quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

    “Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

    Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

    Recent findings suggest that “This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have massive pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most key and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

    The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

    “It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

    In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

    It has been revealed that but when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and remarked he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

    Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

    “Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower remarked.

    According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The fresh clouds, he stated, are made of carbon fiber.

    “These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he remarked.

    Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

    “I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

    Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

    “I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he said, gazing up at it.

    In a recent development, jetBlue is at the moment offering a limited time 125% bonus on purchased points. With this, TrueBlue members can purchase points for as little as 1.43 cents each. Is this a good deal?

    Let’s take a look at the details — so that I don’t bury the lede, let me say that I’d only recommend taking advantage of this JetBlue buy points offer with a specific use in mind, and primarily if you intend to redeem on partner airlines.

    Link: Buy JetBlue TrueBlue points with this promotion with a 125% bonus.

    Between 12AM ET on November 18 and 11:59PM ET on December 31, 2026, JetBlue TrueBlue is offering a bonus on purchased points, which is close to being in line with the best offers from the program.

    JetBlue TrueBlue is offering up to a 125% bonus on purchasing points. The offer is structured as follows, with three tiers of bonuses:.

    JetBlue ordinarily allows TrueBlue members to purchase up to 200,000 points per calendar year. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased to 300,000 points.

    JetBlue ordinarily charges 3.0 cents per purchased point, before the 7.5% federal excise tax. After factoring in the federal excise tax, the standard cost is 3.225 cents per purchased point.

    With this JetBlue points sale, you’d pay the following amounts per purchased point, factoring in the bonus:.

    If you wanted to purchase the fewest possible points at the best possible price, you’d want to purchase a total of 45,000 points (20,000 points plus 25,000 bonus points) at a cost of $645, which gets you the cost of 1.43 cents per point, including all taxes.

    Meanwhile if you wanted to purchase the most possible points, you’d want to purchase a total of 675,000 points (300,000 points plus 375,000 bonus points) at a cost of $9,675, which gets you the same cost per point.

    Industry observers note that officially, JetBlue states that it can take up to 72 hours for purchased points to post. However, in practice (based on my test experience of buying points), they’ll typically post almost instantly. There’s no guarantee of that, though.

    Note that the purchase of JetBlue points is non-refundable, so only make a purchase if you have a specific use in mind. Furthermore, the purchase of JetBlue points doesn’t count toward Mosaic elite status, in case that’s a consideration.

    According to recent reports, when JetBlue does offer a promotion on purchased points, it’s typically in the range of 120-130%. So this is within that range. Personally I’d buy points based on when you’re ready to redeem them, rather than the exact cost. After all, the cost to buy points with a 120% bonus vs. 125% bonus vs. 130% bonus doesn’t differ that much.

    Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

    Sources indicate that jetBlue TrueBlue points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you use a JetBlue credit card to pay for your purchase, it wouldn’t code as a JetBlue purchase.

    Sources indicate that therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See my guide to the best credit cards for buying points.

    JetBlue TrueBlue has become more interesting on the redemption front in recent years, and there are definitely some ways to get outsized value. For that matter, in some cases people may find value in topping off their points balance, in order to have enough points for a redemption.

    Let’s look at the opportunities to redeem TrueBlue points, first for travel on JetBlue, and then for travel on partner airlines. For what it’s worth, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider TrueBlue points to be worth 1.3 cents each.

    When it comes to redeeming on JetBlue, TrueBlue is a revenue based frequent flyer program. That means the cost of an award redemption is correlated to how much a ticket would cost in cash, though it’s not always a consistent cent per point value.

    In my experience, you’ll typically get around 1.3-1.5 cents per TrueBlue point toward the cost of a ticket on JetBlue in economy.

    Just as an example, take a JetBlue flight from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, which costs $334 if paying cash. If redeeming TrueBlue points, you’d pay 22,500 points plus $5.60 in taxes & fees, meaning you’re getting around 1.46 cents of value per point.

    According to recent reports, as another example, take a JetBlue flight from Boston to San Francisco, which has both economy and Mint business class. If paying cash, you’d pay $198 or $676. If redeeming points, you’d pay 14,200 points or 47,300 points, plus $5.60 in taxes & fees, meaning you’re getting around 1.35-1.42 cents of value per point.

    As you can see, these are situations where you probably shouldn’t buy TrueBlue points. For example, there’s no reason to acquire 14,200 points for 1.43 cents each, for a total cost of $203 (plus the $5.60 in taxes & fees), when you could instead just outright buy the ticket for $198.

    One thing to keep in mind is that if you have JetBlue’s most premium card, you can get a 15% award rebate, so maybe there is a little upside there.

    JetBlue TrueBlue has gotten better about adding redemptions on partner airlines in recent times, including on Qatar Airways, Condor, and United Airlines. We’re also now seeing redemptions added on China Airlines. There’s definitely some value to be had here.

    For example, you could redeem just 47,400 points for Condor business class one-way from Frankfurt to Toronto. That’s an amazing opportunity to buy points and immediately get outsized value.

    Sources indicate that as another example, you could redeem 29,600 points for Qatar Airways business class one-way from Munich to Doha. Given the points acquisition costs we’re talking about, that’s an amazing value.

    One caveat I’d just like to add is that partner award availability can be really tough to come by, so only buy points if you have an understanding of what that availability is like.

    In a recent development, as I see it, the decision of whether to buy points from a particular loyalty program comes down both to how valuable that currency is, and it also comes down to how many ways there are to acquire the currency. So that’s why it’s worth mentioning that JetBlue TrueBlue points are really easy to acquire.

    Recent findings suggest that at this point, JetBlue partners with virtually all transferable points currencies, so you can earn TrueBlue points through Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One Rewards, Chase Ultimate Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Wells Fargo, etc. Bilt, Chase, Citi, and Wells Fargo, have 1:1 transfer ratios, while Amex has a 5:4 ratio, and Capital One has a 5:3 ratio.

    It has been revealed that another option is to apply for JetBlue’s co-branded credit cards, which often have large welcome bonuses. Those points of course won’t post anywhere close to instantly, but it’s a good strategy for building up your TrueBlue points balance over time.

    So there’s no shortage of opportunities to earn TrueBlue points — it’s just a function of whether you’d rather part with cash or a points currency.

    Sources indicate that through December 31, 2026, JetBlue is selling TrueBlue points with up to a 125% bonus, an opportunity to buy points for as little as 1.43 cents each. I’d only buy JetBlue points with a specific use in mind. There’s value to be had in some situations, such as if you have a particular Qatar Airways or Condor award you want to book, and there’s availability.
